summary: The Working Families Flexibility Act of 2025 amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to allow private-sector employers to offer compensatory time off instead of monetary overtime compensation, under specific conditions, for a 5-year period.

affected_groups.effect: May choose to receive compensatory time off instead of cash overtime, subject to eligibility and employer agreements, with limits on accrual and protections against coercion.

Allowed to offer compensatory time off in lieu of overtime pay under written or collective bargaining agreements, with rules for cash-outs, termination payouts, and prohibitions against coercing employees.

key_provisions: Eligible private-sector employees who have worked at least 1,000 hours in the previous 12 months may receive compensatory time off at a rate of at least one and one-half hours for each hour of overtime worked, in lieu of monetary pay.
Compensatory time must be provided through a collective bargaining agreement or a voluntary written agreement between the employer and employee made before work is performed.
Employees can accrue a maximum of 160 hours of compensatory time and may request to cash out unused time in writing, which employers must pay within 30 days.
Employers are prohibited from intimidating, threatening, or coercing employees regarding the choice to take compensatory time or use it.
The Comptroller General must submit annual reports to Congress regarding the use of compensatory time, complaints, and enforcement actions over a 4-year period.
The Secretary of Labor must revise employee notice materials within 30 days of enactment to reflect these changes.
missing_information: The exact number of private-sector employees who would choose compensatory time over overtime pay is not specified.
The broader economic impact on total wages or business costs is not provided.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The Working Families Flexibility Act of 2025 amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to allow private-sector employers to offer compensatory time off instead of monetary overtime compensation, under specific conditions, for a 5-year period.
summary_detail.significance: The bill provides private-sector employers and employees the option to utilize compensatory time off instead of mandatory cash overtime for a limited 5-year period, establishing new regulatory reporting requirements and penalties for employer coercion.
